summary: Technical deep dive on Redwood runtime implications for function/tool calling and structured JSON output. Focus on constrained-decoding overhead, batching/KV-cache interactions, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem network impacts. Agreed next steps: run targeted micro-benchmarks, share security docs, and schedule a POC run with Acme's 8k sequence workload.
topics: KV cache warmup and prefix caching
questions: How much overhead does soft-constrained vs hard-constrained decoding add per token?
Does JSON-mode require token-by-token validity checks that block KV cache benefits?
What are practical batching configs for <100ms tail latency with structured output?
How does quantization affect beam/search or nucleus sampling for constrained outputs?
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Park: Ok everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna dive into the runtime perf aspects of tool calling and JSON-mode. We've got Sofia from our infra/SE team and then Acme folks, Jordan, Priya, Sam. Roughly 45 minutes.

[00:18] Jordan Lee: Yep, thanks Alex. We're particularly worried about structured outputs — our downstream systems need valid JSON without heavy postprocessing. We've seen issues where model spits malformed JSON and then our parser fails.

[00:30] Sofia Martinez: Totally — hi all. Quick framing: Redwood supports a "JSON-mode" constrained decoding path where we enforce grammar constraints during generation to guarantee valid JSON (or structured schemas). That can be implemented either as post-hoc repair, a constrained decoding lattice that prunes invalid tokens, or via a guided decoding probability mask. Each has perf tradeoffs.

[00:48] Priya Nair: When you say "guided mask" is that token-level masking every step? I'm worried about the cost per token.

[01:02] Sofia Martinez: Good q. In our implementation for production, the constrained path uses a thin validity-check callback each decoding step. For strict JSON it does a lightweight state machine — it's not a full parser per candidate token, but you do get an extra CPU-bound check per token. For many workloads that's sub-ms, but it adds up at high token rates.

[01:28] Sam O'Connor: Would that kill KV cache benefits? We batch and use prefix caching heavily. If every step needs CPU validation, does that block GPU streaming?

[01:38] Sofia Martinez: Short answer: no, not necessarily. We keep the GPU streaming path for logits and sampling; the JSON validator runs asynchronously on the CPU thread that handles logits postprocessing. The main point of contention is when constrained pruning substantially changes the token distribution, which can increase sampling iterations or require backtracking in some algorithms. But for deterministic mask-based token blocking, we just zero out probs for invalid tokens before sampling, which is cheap.

[02:05] Alex Park: To add to Sofia's point — in our benchmarks we treat constrained decoding as two flavors: soft-guidance (where we bias but don't hard-block) and hard-constrained (where invalid tokens are masked out). Soft-guidance has minimal perf impact, hard constraints add roughly 5-15% wall-clock overhead in token throughput in our mid-size models (for typical JSON schemas).

[02:30] Jordan Lee: Can you quantify that? A percentage is useful but what's the baseline token latency?

[02:36] Sofia Martinez: Sure. On our Dedicated m60-like instance with batch size 1 and quantized execution (Q4_0-style), baseline token emission latency is ~18-25ms per token for a 2k context model with streaming. With hard JSON masking it's more like 20-28ms. For large-batch streaming (batch 8) throughput scales and the per-token amortized latency drops, but tail latencies for the longest sequences can still hit 100-120ms for groups of tokens if caching isn't warm.

[03:10] Priya Nair: That 18-25ms baseline — is that already with KV cache warm? Our workload often does long prefixes and then repeated structured tail generations.

[03:20] Sofia Martinez: The numbers I gave assume KV cache is warm for the current session; cold starts (first generation after model load) double or triple that until KV caches compile slot mappings. We have prefix caching mechanisms to warm common prefixes which we recommend shipping with POC.

[03:34] Sam O'Connor: About batching — we can't always batch across tenants. For our single-tenant VPC on-prem POC we'll likely have lower request parallelism. How should we configure batching vs latency SLOs?

[03:47] Alex Park: For low-concurrency single-tenant workloads, prefer small batch sizes (1-4) and aggressive KV cache usage. Our runtime does continuous batching: it will wait up to a configurable micro-batch time (e.g., 4-8ms) to aggregate requests. Increasing that window improves throughput; lowers cost but raises p95 latency. For a 100ms SLO, we suggest micro-batching <=4ms. For 200ms SLOs, you can push to 10-15ms.

[04:12] Jordan Lee: Ok. Back to constrained decoding — what about function/tool calling? We want the model to emit a JSON object that includes a tool name and arguments. Does the tool-call handshake add overhead?

[04:25] Sofia Martinez: Tool-calling itself is mostly an application-layer protocol. Redwood supports detecting a tool-call token sequence and piping the arguments to your function. The runtime cost is negligible once the output is parsed; the heavy bit is ensuring the emitted arguments are parseable. If you use JSON-mode to guarantee a schema, you get the parse reliability but pay the token-level overhead we discussed. If you do free-text then regex parse, you avoid token overhead but risk fragility and retries.

[04:52] Priya Nair: We run heavy validation on the tool side. Retries from malformed JSON are expensive. Leaning to guarantee correctness at the model stage. But does constrained generation interact poorly with nucleus sampling?

[05:05] Sofia Martinez: Good nuance. Sampling strategies do interact. For top-k/top-p, if you mask out a lot of frequent tokens, the effective entropy drops and you might push sampling into tail tokens, increasing time-to-decision slightly. With nucleus sampling you can observe a small uptick in number of sampling steps if the mask removes many mid-probability tokens. Deterministic decodes (greedy or beam) are more predictable in constrained settings. For critical tooling, we often recommend deterministic or low-temperature settings with hard masking.

[05:36] Alex Park: Also note quantization can change token logits distribution subtly. Quant4-style quant tends to compress logits distribution fidelity; in our internal tests quant4x2 caused a 1-3% change in token rank order for edge tokens which occasionally shifted the first invalid token being proposed and thus changed how the mask applied. Practical impact: small increase in invalid token proposals, which our mask filters out but it slightly increases CPU validation cycles. So if you need absolute parity with float16 sampling, use higher-precision profiles for the model's head.

[06:10] Jordan Lee: So for our POC with 8k sequences, and strict JSON schema, what's the recommended config?

[06:18] Sofia Martinez: For 8k context and structured outputs I'd recommend: quantization: Q4 but test Q8 for head if mismatch; micro-batch window: 4ms for <=100ms SLO; hard masking with deterministic decode for tool calls; pre-warm KV cache with your typical prefixes; run a warmup pass of a few representative prompts across your cluster to populate caches. We'll provide benchmark scripts.

[06:40] Priya Nair: Warmup pass — how long should that be? We're concerned about startup costs on on-prem where GC/OS may evict pages.

[06:48] Sofia Martinez: A couple of minutes per model instance with representative traffic is typically enough to get KV caches and compiled kernels warm. If you're cold-starting often, consider pinning the process or using our Dedicated reserved capacity so instances don't get recycled. On-prem containers can be tuned similarly.

[07:05] Sam O'Connor: Network-wise, if we run Private in our VPC with an on-prem inference node, will the JSON-mode checks introduce noticeable network RTT differences?

[07:15] Alex Park: Network impact is orthogonal: JSON validation is local to the inference node. What affects network is whether you stream tokens (chunked responses) or wait for full response. Streaming reduces client-side perceived latency but increases small packet count. For VPC lanes, monitor egress bandwidth and TCP connection reuse. We can recommend gRPC streaming configs.

[07:36] Jordan Lee: Any gotchas with KV cache and structured output? For repeated similar prompts, sometimes the model starts with a partially-complete JSON and then finishes, causing downstream to see multiple fragments in stream.

[07:49] Sofia Martinez: Streaming fragments are expected. We offer an option to buffer until JSON completes for clients that can't handle partial JSON. That adds latency equal to the time until closing bracket token is emitted. Alternatively, emit delimited JSON objects (one per line) so downstream can process partials safely. Both are application-level tradeoffs.

[08:06] Priya Nair: Can Redwood's runtime do constrained decoding that understands your schema (like required keys) vs only syntactic JSON?

[08:15] Sofia Martinez: We support both levels. Lightweight state-machine for syntactic JSON is cheap. Schema-level constraints (enforcing types, required keys, enum values) means a more complex validator per token — still doable, but costlier. You're trading CPU on the host for reduced app-level validation. In our benchmarks schema-level constraints added another 5-10% overhead compared to syntactic-only for typical schemas.

[08:40] Alex Park: A pattern we've seen is: do syntactic JSON masking in-model, then run schema validation as a post-step but inside the same request flow; if schema validation fails, trigger a constrained repair pass. That avoids always paying full schema-check cost.

[08:58] Jordan Lee: Sounds reasonable. One more question: In terms of observability, can we get token-level metrics showing how often masks pruned top candidates or how many sampling retries occurred?

[09:10] Sofia Martinez: Yes — Redwood Console exposes token-level diagnostics (when enabled): mask-prune-count, sampling-retries, average CPU validation ms per token, and KV-cache hit rate. These can be high-cardinality so they're off by default for privacy/perf, but for POC we'll enable them.

[09:30] Priya Nair: Great. For benchmarking, we want to compare: unconstrained streaming, soft-guidance, hard-mask, and repair-passes. Can you suggest an experiment design?

[09:38] Sofia Martinez: Simple: pick 200 representative prompts covering short/long prefixes and expected JSON sizes. Run each prompt 5x under steady-state warm caches, measuring total wall time, p50/p95/p99 token latency, mask-prune counts, retries, and parsing success rate. Capture exact seeds/sampling params. We'll share a spreadsheet template.

[09:58] Alex Park: We'll also include runs with various quant profiles: Q2/Q4/Q8 and float16 to show fidelity tradeoffs. Expect to see cost savings with Q4 but small parity regressions which you can mitigate by head-precision tuning.

[10:12] Sam O'Connor: Regarding VPC: are there certs or SOC2 docs we need for on-prem? We have a security review next month.

[10:20] Alex Park: I'll send security docs and our private deployment checklist. We support customer-managed KMS/HSM and SSO. For on-prem installs we provide an air-gapped bundle and audit logs.

[10:33] Jordan Lee: Awesome. Any closing recommendations for our initial POC config?

[10:38] Sofia Martinez: Recap suggestion: Dedicated/private on-prem node using Q4 quant, hard JSON masking with deterministic decode for tool calls, micro-batch 1-4 with 4ms window, pre-warm KV cache with your prompt set, capture token-level diagnostics. If you see parsing failures, run schema-level repair passes on failed responses.

[10:58] Priya Nair: Sounds good. We'll share prompt set by EOD Friday.

[11:03] Alex Park: Great — action items noted. We'll follow up with the benchmark template and security docs. Thanks everyone.

[11:10] Speaker 1: (crosstalk) thanks

[11:15] End of call.
